evidence.quote: A1.5 M stoichiometric perovskite precursor solution was obtained by dissolving MAI (1.5M) and PbI2 (1.5 M) in a mixed solvent of DMF:DMSO = 10:1 (v:v). 2 mol % or 5 mol % PbI2 was added into a stoichiometric MAPbI3 perovskite solution to form MAPbI3 films with excess PbI2. The MAPbI3 films were deposited on the pre-fabricated SnO2/ITO substrates by a one-step spin-coating process: keeping 4,000 rpm for 30 s and dropping 400 m L of antisolvent (e.g., diethyl ether) at the 23 rd s to form wet perovskite precursor films after spin coating. After that, the as-prepared perovskite films were annealed on a hot plate at 100  C for 10 min in an N2filled glovebox.

Encouraged by the above results, we then investigated the influences of Pb 0 on the efficiency and stability of PSCs. The light-aged PbI2 films loaded with Pb 0 impurities on purpose were employed to assemble perovskite films and devices. The perovskite films were fabricated by a two-step deposition method, as illustrated in Figure 3A. The devices used SnO2 as electron transfer layers and 2,20,7,70-tetrakis [N,N-di(4-methoxyphenyl) amino]-9,90-spiro-bifluorene (spiro-OMeTAD) as holetransfer layers. In the first step, we employed PbI2 films with light irradiation for different times (e.g., 2, 4, 6, and 8 h) and fresh PbI2 as control sample as precursor layers.

To explore the origins of performance degradation, we performed PL and TRPL analysis to estimate the carrier recombination in perovskite films. As shown in Figures 4A and 4B, all the samples exhibited a PL peak at about 805 nm, indicating that the main components remained FA1 � xMAxPbI3 perovskites even though using light-aged PbI2 as the precursor layer. Whereas the gradually decreased PL peak of the lightaged PbI2-based samples manifests that the Pb 0 serving as traps to capture carriers would lead to severely photogenerated charge carrier recombination.

A 1.4 M stoichiometric perovskite precursor solution was obtained by dissolving PbI2, PbBr2, MABr, FAI, and CsI with 1 mol % KI additive in a mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO (4:1/v:v). Extra 5 mol % PbI2 was added into the stoichiometric mixed-cation perovskite solution for the excess PbI2. For BABr solution, BABr was dissolved into IPA solvent with a concentration of 2 mg/mL. The perovskite films (with or without excess PbI2) were deposited on the pre-fabricated SnO2/ITO substrates by a two-step spin-coating process: first at 1,000 rpm for 5 s with a ramp of 5,000 rpm/s, and then at 5,000 rpm for 45 s with a ramp of 10,000 rpm/s.

We then used these films for the fabrication of solar cells and investigated their effects on device performance. The devices employed a planar n-i-p structure using SnO2 as an electron-transport layer and spiro-OMeTAD as a hole-transfer layer. The detail of the fabrication process is described in the experimental procedures section. J-V characteristics and photovoltaic parameters of the corresponding PSCs are shown in Figures 5E, 5F, and S21 and Tables 2 and S3. The presence of excess PbI2 in PSCs improved FF from 76.0% to 80.2% and PCE from 20.1% to 21.2% (Figure 5E).
